paragraphs.text:
In the classical model for ordinary thermal conditions, this motion is ongoing and irregular.
Experimental evidence supports these ideas within their ranges of applicability.
This introductory model does not mean that every particle always follows a classical random trajectory under every condition, especially in very cold or extremely dense matter.

Thermal processes are connected with the internal structure of matter.
For example, heating a piece of paraffin to a temperature of a few tens of degrees Celsius can melt it.
An iron rod heated to the same temperature remains solid, although it warms and can expand.

The different responses are related to the materials' internal structures and interactions.
Studying thermal phenomena helps us understand matter's structure.
In turn, a model of that structure helps explain the physical nature of thermal phenomena.

The textbook ranges from the thin gas in the upper atmosphere to solids on Earth and the very dense cores of planets and stars.
In these settings, matter's properties depend on its constituent particles, their motion, and their interactions.
Depending on the material and conditions, the relevant particles may be molecules, atoms①, or smaller charged particles.

Not every material consists of separate molecules.
At extreme temperatures or densities, atoms and molecules may no longer remain intact, and a simple classical molecular model may be insufficient.

① An atom is the smallest unit that retains the chemical identity of an element.
For a molecular substance, a molecule is a discrete, electrically neutral group of bonded atoms that retains that substance's molecular identity.
This does not mean that one isolated molecule has every bulk property of a macroscopic sample.
The molecular description is not a definition that treats ionic or metallic solids as collections of separate molecules.
